explanations.explanation: Armies it is, friend. Jabin, king of Hazor, sent word to the other kings, and they "…came out with all their armies, a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore…" (Joshua 11:1, 4). Kings from the mountains, the foothills, the Arabah and beyond all showed up. You know how hard it is to get a whole family to agree on one dinner time? These kings got ALL those armies to one place!

Treasures aren't on the list. The text says the kings came out with all their armies, along with a great number of horses and chariots. Hauling treasure to a battle would be like showing up to a big job with your best serving tray and no tools. I think these kings had fighting on their minds.

The text never mentions priests in this march. What it does say is that the kings came out with all their armies, along with horses and chariots. I think that tells us what was on their minds. This crowd came to fight.

Merom, friend. Verse 5 says the kings joined forces and encamped at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel. They all parked in one spot, and that spot is where the battle comes to them. Remember that name, because you'll see it again.

Close to the right neighborhood, but the text names a different spot. Joshua 11:5 says the kings encamped at the waters of Merom. That's where they gathered to fight against Israel. Gilgal isn't in this chapter's camp at all.

The Valley of Elah belongs to a whole other story, where Saul, Israel's king, and the men of Israel camped to face the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:2). Here, Joshua 11:5 says the kings joined forces and encamped at the waters of Merom. Two camps, two stories. It's easy to mix them up, so no crumbs to be embarrassed about.

explanations.answer: Do not be afraid of them
explanations.explanation: That's the very first thing He says: "Do not be afraid of them…" Look at the size of that army, then look at those words. The LORD gives Joshua a plan right after, and Joshua doesn't have to guess what comes next. When the LORD says don't be afraid, that settles it.

explanations.answer: Do not go out against them
explanations.explanation: The LORD never tells Joshua to stay put. He says, "Do not be afraid of them…" and then tells him what to do about their horses and chariots. Joshua and his army come upon the kings suddenly and attack (Joshua 11:7). That's the opposite of staying home.

The LORD doesn't say to hold off. He starts with "Do not be afraid of them…" and then says that by this time tomorrow He will deliver all of them slain before Israel (Joshua 11:6). That promise is about when He delivers them. Then Joshua and his army come upon the kings suddenly and attack (Joshua 11:7).

Burn them up, that's the word. The LORD says, "You are to hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots." Verse 9 says Joshua did exactly that. The chariots go up in flames, so nobody gets them back.

No, the chariots don't get added to Israel's collection. The LORD tells Joshua to burn them up. Verse 9 says Joshua treated the horses and chariots as the LORD had told him. A chariot with a fresh coat of ash isn't much of a prize.
The LORD doesn't say to leave them there. His word to Joshua is to burn up their chariots (Joshua 11:6). And verse 9 says Joshua burned them up. Burning is the order, friend, not parking.

The text never says Israel was bigger. It says the kings' armies were a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore (Joshua 11:4). What it does say is that the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel (Joshua 11:8). So the win comes from Him, not from Israel's headcount.

False is right. Nothing in the text says Israel had more soldiers. The kings brought a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore (Joshua 11:4). Joshua 11:8 says the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel. The battle was won by the LORD's hand, not by headcount.

True, baker! The LORD told Joshua to hamstring the horses and burn up the chariots (Joshua 11:6). Then verse 9 says Joshua treated them as the LORD had told him. No tweaking, no "close enough." I've been known to eyeball the flour and call it a day, so this kind of follow-through impresses me.

It's actually true, friend. Joshua 11:9 says he treated them as the LORD had told him, so he hamstrung their horses and burned up their chariots. That matches what the LORD said in verse 6. Joshua didn't change a thing.

explanations.answer: It had been the head of all these kingdoms
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. Verse 10 says Hazor "…was formerly the head of all these kingdoms." It was the top city of the bunch. So when Joshua turns back, he's going straight to the head.

explanations.answer: It had the strongest walls in the whole north
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about walls. It gives one reason: Hazor was formerly the head of all these kingdoms (Joshua 11:10). I'd love to tell you more about the stonework, but the verse doesn't. Hazor was the head, and that's why Joshua turns back.

explanations.answer: It sat the closest to the camp of Israel
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the chapter says Hazor was the closest. Joshua 11:10 says Joshua turned back to Hazor because it was formerly the head of all these kingdoms. The text gives distance no part in it. It was about who led the rest.

Yes. Verse 12 says Joshua captured all these kings and their cities and put them to the sword. He devoted them to destruction, as Moses the LORD's servant had commanded. That's a big sweep, and it's a heavy part of the story.

No deals on the table here. Joshua 11:12 says Joshua captured all these kings and their cities and put them to the sword. He did it as Moses the LORD's servant had commanded. And verse 19 says no city made peace except the Hivites living in Gibeon.

explanations.answer: He lets them keep their land
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. Joshua captured all these kings and their cities (Joshua 11:12). He devoted them to destruction as Moses the LORD's servant had commanded. Only the Hivites of Gibeon made peace (Joshua 11:19).
True. Verse 13 says Israel did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds, except Hazor, which Joshua burned. Hazor is the one exception on that list. I'd call that a very specific detail.

It's true, friend. Verse 13 says, "Yet Israel did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds, except Hazor, which Joshua burned." So Hazor stands alone on that list. Good thing the verse is clear, because I almost second-guessed it myself.

Nothing at all. Verse 15 says Joshua did it all, "…leaving nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses." Moses, Israel's leader before Joshua, passed the command on, and Joshua carried it out. Picture a to-do list with every box checked.

Not even a little. Joshua 11:15 says he left "…nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses." Moses, Israel's leader before Joshua, passed the command along, and Joshua followed it. If I had that record, I'd frame it and hang it in the bakery.

Half would be a pretty big gap. But Joshua 11:15 says he left "…nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses." Moses, Israel's leader before Joshua, had passed the command on to him. Joshua finished all of it.
The text says otherwise. Verse 18 says Joshua waged war against all these kings "…for a long period of time." So this wasn't wrapped up in a few days. The chapter covers a long stretch of fighting.
False is right. Joshua 11:18 says he waged war against all these kings "…for a long period of time." So this wasn't wrapped up in a few days. Taking that whole region took a long stretch.

The Hivites living in Gibeon. Verse 19 says no city made peace with the Israelites except them, and all others were taken in battle. Out of the whole region, one city made peace. That tells you how rare it was.

The Jebusites show up in verse 3 as one of the peoples in the hill country that Jabin sent word to. But the one that made peace is named in verse 19: the Hivites living in Gibeon. So that's the only city on the list. Jerusalem isn't mentioned in the verse.
Jericho isn't named in this part of the story. Verse 19 names one city that made peace with the Israelites: the Hivites living in Gibeon. All others were taken in battle. Gibeon is the answer.

Gaza, Gath and Ashdod, baker! Verse 22 says no Anakim were left in the land of the Israelites, "only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod did any survive." Verse 21 has Joshua clearing them out of the hill country, and then this little list is all that's left. Three cities. You picked them out like a pro.

Close, friend, but those names come from the verse right before. Verse 21 says Joshua eliminated the Anakim from the hill country of Hebron, Debir and Anab. The survivors come in verse 22: Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. Two verses back to back, like two cookie tins that look the same. Easy to reach for the first tin on the shelf.

Jericho, Ai and Bethel are names you might know from other parts of Joshua, but they aren't in this list. Joshua 11:22 says the Anakim who survived were in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod. Those three are the only ones named here. When a verse hands you a short list, stick to the list, friend.

Inheritance, friend. Verse 23 says Joshua "…gave it as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes." It's the kind of thing handed down, the way a family keeps the good recipe. The land was given out by allotments to the tribes.

An offering is something you give away, but verse 23 goes the other direction. It says Joshua gave the land "…as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes." The land is given to Israel, each tribe by its allotment. That's the word to remember.

Tribute is something paid in, but that isn't what's happening here. Joshua 11:23 says he gave the land "…as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes." The land is handed to Israel, tribe by tribe. The word you want is inheritance.
